meta.note: New in Academy v2. Scenarios use fictional situations; no real client names or figures.

challenges.title: The account manager's email
challenges.situation: A Business Relationship Manager (BRM) forwards a client email: 'Can you run a fun workshop for our staff next month?' No problem statement, no sponsor, no budget.
challenges.question: What is your best first move?

options.text: Book the date and send a workshop agenda template.
options.feedback: A workshop is a format, not an answer. You would be solving an unframed problem.

options.text: Call the BRM to find the trigger behind the request: what changed, who is asking, what decision must follow.
options.feedback: Yes. CoDesign starts from the trigger and the decision it should support. The format comes later.

options.text: Reply that CoDesign only works on large bids.
options.feedback: Small requests can hide real opportunities. Qualify before you decline.

options.text: Ask an AI agent to write a proposal straight away.
options.feedback: The agent can help once you know the challenge. Without it, the draft is generic.

challenges.title: Reframe the brief
challenges.situation: The client asks to 'reinvent the employee restaurant'. You learn attendance is down and teams no longer meet in person.
challenges.question: Which reframed challenge is strongest?

options.text: How might we redesign the restaurant menu?
options.feedback: Too narrow: it assumes the menu is the problem.

options.text: How might we make the office day worth the commute, with food as one lever?
options.feedback: Right. It widens to the experience while keeping food in scope, which is what Presales is for.

options.text: How might we increase restaurant revenue by 20%?
options.feedback: A business target is useful, but this framing loses the user and invents a figure.

options.text: How might we digitise everything?
options.feedback: Solution-first and vague. Reframe around a user moment.

challenges.title: Forty logos, three slots
challenges.situation: You pitch to a hospital group about the patient meal experience. Your most impressive credential is an airport lounge project.
challenges.question: How do you use the lounge credential?

options.text: Leave it out: it is not healthcare.
options.feedback: Possibly, but you may lose a strong method proof. Sector is not the only criterion.

options.text: Show it as 'how we redesign a time-pressured service moment' and say clearly what transfers and what does not.
options.feedback: Yes. Select on user moment and constraint, lead with a method proof, and be explicit about transfer limits.

options.text: Show it first with its contract value to impress.
options.feedback: Contract values are internal and unverified for external use. Impressive is not the same as relevant.

options.text: Rename it as a healthcare project.
options.feedback: Never. A credential must trace to an approved source.

challenges.title: The leading question
challenges.situation: Your interview guide includes: 'Don't you think the queue at lunch is too long?'
challenges.question: What is wrong, and how do you fix it?

options.text: Nothing; it confirms a known pain point.
options.feedback: It leads the answer. You will collect agreement, not insight.

options.text: Replace it with: 'Tell me about the last time you had lunch here. What happened?'
options.feedback: Open, past-behaviour questions surface real stories and pain points you did not expect.

options.text: Make it a 1–5 rating question.
options.feedback: A survey item can help, but it does not replace an open interview question.

options.text: Ask it twice to be sure.
options.feedback: Repetition does not fix bias.

challenges.title: Persona or stereotype?
challenges.situation: A draft persona reads: 'Paul, 45, male, likes football and burgers.'
challenges.question: What would make this a useful persona?

options.text: Add a stock photo and a fun quote.
options.feedback: Decoration, not evidence. The persona still says nothing about behaviour.

options.text: Base it on behaviours, goals and frictions seen in research, each trait traced to an interview or observation.
options.feedback: Yes. Behaviour-based and evidence-traced personas drive design decisions; demographics rarely do.

options.text: Create ten more personas to cover everyone.
options.feedback: More personas dilute focus. Three to five behaviour-based ones are usually enough.

options.text: Ask an AI to invent the details.
options.feedback: AI can structure a synthesis, but invented traits are fiction. Trace every trait.

challenges.title: Where is the pain?
challenges.situation: Your journey map has seven stages and lists every touchpoint, but the team cannot agree where to focus.
challenges.question: What is missing?

options.text: More stages.
options.feedback: Granularity is not the issue.

options.text: Evidence-backed pain points and emotions per stage, and a few marked priority moments.
options.feedback: Right. A journey map exists to show where it hurts and which moments matter most.

options.text: A nicer colour scheme.
options.feedback: Visual quality matters, but it will not create focus.

options.text: The future journey.
options.feedback: The future journey comes in Co-create, after you know the priority moments.

challenges.title: Seven days before
challenges.situation: Participants arrive at the workshop without having read anything, and the first hour is spent explaining context.
challenges.question: Which block would have prevented this?

options.text: Annexes (06.04)
options.feedback: Annexes archive outputs after the project.

options.text: Pre-read J-7 (04.05), possibly with the Mini Podcast (04.06)
options.feedback: Yes. A short pre-read seven days before, plus a podcast for busy people, lets the workshop start on decisions.

options.text: Benchmark (03.04)
options.feedback: Benchmarks inspire, but they do not brief participants.

options.text: Value Proposition Workshop (06.03)
options.feedback: That comes much later in the process.

challenges.title: The senior voice
challenges.situation: During ideation, a senior director talks for ten minutes and the group nods along.
challenges.question: What is your best facilitation move?

options.text: Let it run: they are the decision maker.
options.feedback: You lose the diversity of ideas that co-creation is for.

options.text: Switch to silent individual ideation for five minutes, then round-robin sharing.
options.feedback: Yes. 'Write before you speak' and structured turns protect quieter voices without confronting anyone.

options.text: Ask the director to leave.
options.feedback: Too confrontational. Use structure, not exclusion.

options.text: End the session early.
options.feedback: The problem is the format, not the session.

challenges.title: AI ideas on the wall
challenges.situation: You have 20 AI-generated ideas ready. The workshop starts in five minutes.
challenges.question: When and how do you use them?

options.text: Show all 20 first so people have a starting point.
options.feedback: This anchors the group on AI output and kills original thinking.

options.text: Run human ideation first, then bring a few AI ideas as stimuli to extend or challenge the wall, labelled as AI.
options.feedback: Right. Human-led, AI-supported: AI ideas widen the space after people have contributed.

options.text: Present them as the client team's ideas.
options.feedback: Never mislabel sources.

options.text: Don't mention they exist.
options.feedback: Prepared stimuli are useful. Use them transparently at the right moment.

challenges.title: The summary nobody reads
challenges.situation: Your workshop summary is a 40-slide photo dump of every sticky note.
challenges.question: What should page one say?

options.text: A thank-you message and the agenda.
options.feedback: Polite but useless for decisions.

options.text: Decided / To validate / Discarded, each with an owner and a date.
options.feedback: Yes. A summary turns workshop energy into owned decisions.

options.text: The full list of participants.
options.feedback: Useful in an annex, not on page one.

options.text: The best quotes from the day.
options.feedback: Quotes can bring colour, but decisions come first.

challenges.title: Everything is a priority
challenges.situation: After voting, 14 of 18 ideas are tagged 'high priority'.
challenges.question: What do you do?

options.text: Accept it: the client loves the ideas.
options.feedback: If everything is a priority, nothing is.

options.text: Score them against agreed, weighted criteria (impact, feasibility, effort) and show the breakdown, then let people challenge it.
options.feedback: Right. Transparent criteria make the trade-offs explicit and defensible.

options.text: Pick your own favourites.
options.feedback: Prioritisation must be shared and traceable, not imposed.

options.text: Ask an AI to choose.
options.feedback: AI can score against criteria you set, but people own the decision.

challenges.title: Capture the credential
challenges.situation: The project ended last week. The final restitution deck is approved.
challenges.question: What is the right credential capture move?

options.text: Wait until someone asks for it in a bid.
options.feedback: Memory fades and files move. Capture while the evidence is fresh.

options.text: Draft a credential card with the Credential Writer agent, mark every unverified figure, and get sharing approval.
options.feedback: Yes. A credential proves a project is referenced; figures need a source and approval before reuse.

options.text: Copy the client's logo and the contract value into the library.
options.feedback: Logos and amounts need approval. The story is the challenge, approach and outputs.

options.text: Write it from memory in two lines.
options.feedback: Too thin to reuse, and not traceable.

quests.title: The hybrid HQ
quests.brief: A fictional global bank (Northbridge Financial) wants its regional HQ to be 'worth the commute'. Attendance is 2.4 days a week; lunch queues break the team moment.
quests.ask: Shortlist three credentials for the first meeting.
quests.lesson: Lead with hybrid rhythms and workplace dining (Microsoft, J&J, Santander, Thales). A greenfield factory is less relevant to a hybrid office.

quests.title: Matchday under pressure
quests.brief: A fictional stadium (Riverside) loses fans at half-time: 15-minute queues for food and drinks, and families feel unwelcome.
quests.lesson: Matchday and event F&B flows (Newcastle, Roland-Garros) prove the method directly. Arsenal Women adds a supporter-diversity angle.

quests.title: The patient meal
quests.brief: A fictional hospital group (St Aldric) wants to improve the patient meal experience: cold trays, little choice, meals at fixed times.
quests.lesson: Clariane and HSTV Moncontour redesign mealtime in care settings. Say openly that care homes are not acute wards: lead with the method and the resident journey, not the numbers.

quests.title: The campus without a credential
quests.brief: A fictional university (Lakeshore) wants students to eat on campus rather than off-site. There is no verified education credential in the library.
quests.ask: Shortlist three cross-sector credentials and say why they transfer.
quests.lesson: No education credential exists: say so. Use multi-site campus dining (Thales, AstraZeneca), multi-audience flows (European Parliament) and Seazon, whose co-design explicitly covered students.

glossary.definition: How Might We — an opportunity question that frames a problem so it invites many solutions.
Business Relationship Manager — the account owner who often brings the opportunity.
CoDesign OS — the agent platform that drafts CoDesign artefacts. Human-led, AI-supported.
Discover and Define (diverge then converge on the problem), then Co-create and Test & Deliver (diverge then converge on the solution). Presales precedes it.
A behaviour-based archetype built from research evidence, not demographics.
Stages, actions, emotions and pain points of a persona over time, with priority moments marked.
A journey map extended with front-stage and back-stage processes, people and systems.
Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, Informed — who does what on the engagement.
A short briefing sent seven days before a workshop so the session can start on decisions.
Format A: half-day workshop (09:00–13:00, 240 min). Format B: full day (09:00–17:00, 480 min).
Cumulative competency levels: Aware, Contributor, Facilitator, Practitioner, Lead / Faculty. Attending a session never grants N3.
A referenced past project. It proves the project exists, not that a deliverable or impact is approved for reuse.
Activities → outputs → outcomes → measures, used to design pilots and business cases.
A one-page description of an idea from the workshop, in participants' own words.
A stimulus card showing an in-sector or out-of-sector example to spark ideas.
A developed direction that links a need and evidence to an idea, value and next test.
Jobs To Be Done — what a person is trying to get done, independent of the solution.
Academy reward for learning activity (Spark → Faculty-ready). Separate from N-levels, which a coach certifies.
